title: An Achilles' Heel, of Sorts
gist_ar: نص ساخر عن الإفراط في الإشارات الثقافية: الكاتب بيسخر من الأسلوب اللي بيستخدمه.
text:
It has become the eleventh hour for a certain kind of business prose, and one can only hope the Rubicon has been crossed.

Consider the following, from a strategy document I am not at liberty to name. The company's legacy systems are described as an Achilles' heel; migrating them is a Herculean task; the vendor's proposal is a Trojan horse; and the whole situation constitutes a catch-22 which, if resolved at all, will be a Pyrrhic victory. Four allusions and a paradox in ninety words, and not one of them conjures anything, because they have been invoked so often that the imagery has worn through to the metaphor beneath.

The tongue-in-cheek defence is that this is a shared vocabulary, and there is something in it. An allusion that lands does real work: it imports a whole narrative in two syllables, and the resonance is genuinely economical. But resonance requires that something be resonating. An Achilles' heel is a vulnerability in an otherwise invulnerable thing, and the legacy systems in question were, by the document's own account, weak throughout. The allusion is not merely tired; it is wrong, and it is wrong in a way that flatters the subject.

That is the fine point, and it is not a matter of taste. The layered meaning of a good allusion constrains what you may say with it. Use one carelessly and it will smuggle in a claim you did not make — here, that everything else was sound.

There is a subtext to prose of this kind, and the motif is unmistakable once you look: each phrase juxtaposes a heroic register against an administrative problem. Somebody wanted the migration to feel like a siege. I have no doubt it felt like one. But wit is not the same as allusion, and the document, which is witty nowhere, alludes constantly.

questions.q: What is the writer's central criticism of the allusions?
options: They are worn out and one of them is factually wrong in a flattering way
They are far too obscure for a business audience to recognise or understand at all
There are not enough of them to sustain the argument

questions.q: Why is 'Achilles' heel' the wrong allusion here?
questions.q_ar: ليه 'نقطة ضعف أخيل' إشارة غلط هنا؟
options: It implies the rest was invulnerable, and the systems were weak throughout
Achilles was not vulnerable at the heel
It is too literary for a strategy document

questions.q: What does he say a careless allusion smuggles in?
questions.q_ar: بيقول إن الإشارة المتسرّعة بتدخّل إيه؟
options: A claim you did not make

questions.q: What is the sting in the final sentence?
options: The document alludes constantly but is witty nowhere
The migration was genuinely heroic, and the allusions therefore fit it well
The writer admits he cannot name the document
